hieroglyphical.c: Hieroglyphical Hieroglyphic { Hi`er*o*glyph"ic (?), Hi`er*o*glyph"ic*al (?), } a. [L. hieroglyphicus, Gr.?; "iero`s sacred + gly`fein to carve: cf. F. hiéroglyphique.]

hieroglyphist.c: Hieroglyphist Hi`er*og"ly*phist (?; 277), n. One versed in hieroglyphics. Gliddon.

hierogram.c: Hierogram Hi"er*o*gram (?), n. [Gr. "iero`s sacred + -gram.] A form of sacred or hieratic writing.

hierogrammatic.c: Hierogrammatic Hi`er*o*gram"mat"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. hiérogrammatique.] Written in, or pertaining to, hierograms; expressive of sacred writing. Bp. Warburton.

hierogrammatist.c: Hierogrammatist Hi`er*o*gram"ma*tist (?), n. [Cf. F. hiérogrammatiste.] A writer of hierograms; also, one skilled in hieroglyphics. Greenhill.

hierographical.c: Hierographical Hierographic { Hi`er*o*graph"ic (?), Hi`er*o*graph"ic*al (?), } a. [L. hierographicus, Gr.?: cf. F. hiérographique.] Of or pertaining to sacred writing.

hierography.c: Hierography Hi`er*og"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr.?; "iero`s sacred +? to write: cf. F. hiérographie.] Sacred writing. [R.] Bailey.

hierolatry.c: Hierolatry Hi`er*ol"a*try (?), n. [Gr. "iero`s sacred +? worship,? to worship.] The worship of saints or sacred things. [R.] Coleridge.

hierological.c: Hierological Hierologic { Hi`er*o*log"ic (?), Hi`er*o*log"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. hiérologique.] Pertaining to hierology.

hierologist.c: Hierologist Hi`er*ol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in, or whostudies, hierology.

hierology.c: Hierology Hi`er*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.?; "iero`s sacred +? discourse: cf. F. hiérologie.] A treatise on sacred things; especially, the science which treats of the ancient writings and inscriptions of the Egyptians, or a treatise on that science.

hieromancy.c: Hieromancy Hi"er*o*man`cy (?), n. [Gr. "iero`s sacred +? divination: cf. F. hiéromantie.] Divination by observing the objects offered in sacrifice.

hieromartyr.c: Hieromartyr Hi"er*o*mar`tyr (?), n. [Gr. "iero`s sacred + E. martyr.] A priest who becomes a martyr.

hieromnemon.c: Hieromnemon ‖Hi`e*rom*ne"mon (?), n. [NL., from Gr.?; "iero`s sacred +? mindful, fr.? to think on, remember.] (Gr. Antiq.) 1. The sacred secretary or recorder sent by each state belonging to the Amphictyonic Council, along with the deputy or minister. Liddel & Scott.

hieron.c: Hieron ‖Hi"er*on (?), n. [Gr. "iero`n.] A consecrated place; esp., a temple.

hieronymite.c: Hieronymite Hi`er*on"y*mite (?), n. [From St. Hieronymus, or Jerome.] (Eccl.) See Jeronymite.

hierophant.c: Hierophant Hi*er"o*phant (hi*ĕr"o*faint or hī"ẽr; 277), n. [L. hierophanta, hierophantes, Gr. "ierofa`nths; "iero`s sacred + fai`nein to show, make known: cf. F. hiérophante.] The presiding priest who initiated candidates at the Eleusinian mysteries; hence, one who teaches the mysteries and duties of a religion or an arcane discipline; an expositor; as, In his television series “Cosmos”, Carl Sagan became the foremost hierophant of modern cosmology.. Abp. Potter.

hierophantic.c: Hierophantic Hi`er*o*phan"tic (?), a. [Gr. "ierofantiko`s.] Of or relating to hierophants or their teachings.

hieroscopy.c: Hieroscopy Hi`er*os"co*py (?), n. [Gr. "ieroskopi`a divination; "iero`s sacred +? to view.] Divination by inspection of entrails of victims offered in sacrifice.

hierotheca.c: Hierotheca ‖Hi`er*o*the"ca (?), n.; pl. -cæ (#). [NL., fr. Gr.?; "iero`s sacred +? chest.] A receptacle for sacred objects.

hierourgy.c: Hierourgy Hi"er*our`gy (?), n. [Gr.?; "iero`s sacred +? work.] A sacred or holy work or worship. [Obs.] Waterland.

higgle.c: Higgle Hig"gle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Higgled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Higgling (?).] [Cf. Haggle, or Huckster.] 1. To hawk or peddle provisions.

higgledypiggledy.c: Higgledy-piggledy Hig`gle*dy-pig"gle*dy (?), adv. In confusion; topsy-turvy. [Colloq.] Johnson.

high.c: High High (?), v. i. [See Hie.] To hie. [Obs.]

High High (?), a. [Compar. Higher (?); superl. Highest.] [OE. high, hegh, hey, heh, AS. heáh, h?h; akin to OS. h?h, OFries. hag, hach, D. hoog, OHG. h?h, G. hoch, Icel. h?r, Sw. hög, Dan. höi, Goth. hauhs, and to Icel. haugr mound, G. hügel hill, Lith. kaukaras.] 1. Elevated above any starting point of measurement, as a line, or surface; having altitude; lifted up; raised or extended in the direction of the zenith; lofty; tall; as, a high mountain, tower, tree; the sun is high.

High High (?), adv. In a high manner; in a high place; to a great altitude; to a great degree; largely; in a superior manner; eminently; powerfully. “And reasoned high.” Milton. “I can not reach so high.” Shak.
High High, n. 1. An elevated place; a superior region; a height; the sky; heaven.
High High (?), v. i. To rise; as, the sun higheth. [Obs.]
High five High five. 1. See Cinch (the game).
High priest High" priest` (?). (Eccl.) A chief priest; esp., the head of the Jewish priesthood.
High steel High steel. Steel containing a high percentage of carbon; high-carbon steel.

highbinder.c: Highbinder High"bind`er (?), n. A ruffian; one who hounds, or spies upon, another; app. esp. to the members of certain alleged societies among the Chinese. [U. S.]

highblown.c: High-blown High"-blown` (?), a. Inflated, as with conceit.

highborn.c: Highborn High"born` (?), a. Of noble or aristocratic birth. Contrasted with lowborn and common. Shak.

highboy.c: Highboy High"boy`, n. 1. One who lives high; also, in politics, a highflyer.

highbred.c: High-bred High"-bred` (?), a. Bred in high life; of pure blood. Byron.

highbuilt.c: High-built High"-built` (?), a. Of lofty structure; tall. “High-built organs.” Tennyson.

highchurch.c: High-church High"-church` (?), a. Of or pertaining to, or favoring, the party called the High Church, or their doctrines or policy. See High Church, under High, a.

highchurchism.c: High-churchism High"-church`ism (?), n. The principles of the high-church party.

highchurchman.c: High-churchman High"-church`man (?), n.; pl. -men (?). One who holds high-church principles.

highchurchmanship.c: High-churchman-ship High"-church`man-ship, n. The state of being a high-churchman. J. H. Newman.

highcolored.c: High-colored High"-col`ored (?), a. 1. Having a strong, deep, or glaring color; flushed. Shak.

highembowed.c: High-embowed High"-em*bowed ` (?), a. Having lofty arches. “The high-embowed roof.” Milton.

higher.c: Higher criticism High"er crit"i*cism. Criticism which includes the study of the contents, literary character, date, authorship, etc., of any writing; as, the higher criticism of the Pentateuch. Called also historical criticism.
Higher thought Higher thought. See New thought, below.

higherup.c: higher-up high"er-up", n. A superior officer or official; a person having greater rank or station or quality than others; -- used chiefly in pl. [Slang]

highfaluting.c: highfaluting highfalutin high`fa*lu"tin, high`fa*lu"ting (?), n. [Perh. a corruption of highflighting.] High-flown, bombastic language. [Written also hifalutin.] [Jocular, U. S.] Lowell.

highfinished.c: High-finished High"-fin`ished (?), a. Finished with great care; polished.

highflier.c: Highflier High"fli`er (?), n. 1. One who is extravagant in pretensions, opinions, or manners; one who is highfaluting. Swift.

highflown.c: High-flown High"-flown` (?), a. 1. Elevated; proud. “High-flown hopes.” Denham.

highflying.c: Highflying High"fly`ing (?), a. 1. Extravagant in opinions or ambition. “Highflying, arbitrary kings.” Dryden.

highgo.c: High-go High"-go` (?), n. A spree; a revel. [Low]

highhanded.c: High-handed High"-hand`ed (?), a. Overbearing; oppressive; arbitrary; violent; as, a high-handed act.

highhearted.c: High-hearted High"-heart`ed (?), a. Full of courage or nobleness; high-souled. -- High"-heart`ed*ness, n.

highhoe.c: High-hoe High"-hoe` (?), n. (Zool.) The European green woodpecker or yaffle. [Written also high-hoo.]

highholder.c: High-holder High"-hold`er (?), n. (Zool.) The flicker; -- called also high-hole. [Local, U. S.]

highland.c: Highland High"land (?), n. Elevated or mountainous land; (often in the pl.) an elevated region or country; as, the Highlands of Scotland.

highlow.c: High-low High"-low` (?), n. A laced boot, ankle high.

highly.c: Highly High"ly, adv. In a high manner, or to a high degree; very much; as, highly esteemed.

highmen.c: Highmen High"men (?), n. pl. Loaded dice so contrived as to turn up high numbers. [Obs] Sir J. Harrington.

highmettled.c: High-mettled High"-met`tled (?), a. Having abundance of mettle; ardent; full of fire; as, a high-mettled steed.

highmindedness.c: High-mindedness High"-mind`ed*ness, n. The quality of being highminded; nobleness; magnanimity.

highness.c: Highness High"ness, n. [AS. heáhnes.] 1. The state of being high; elevation; loftiness.

highpalmed.c: High-palmed High"-palmed` (?), a. (Zool.) Having high antlers; bearing full-grown antlers aloft.

highpressure.c: High-pressure High"-pres`sure (?; 135), a. 1. Having or involving a pressure greatly exceeding that of the atmosphere; -- said of steam, air, water, etc., and of steam, air, or hydraulic engines, water wheels, etc.

highpriesthood.c: High-priesthood High"-priest`hood (?), n. The office, dignity, or position of a high priest.

highprincipled.c: High-principled High"-prin`ci*pled (?), a. Possessed of noble or honorable principles.

highproof.c: High-proof High"-proof` (?), a. 1. Highly rectified; very strongly alcoholic; as, high-proof spirits.

highraised.c: High-raised High"-raised` (?), a. 1. Elevated; raised aloft; upreared.

highreaching.c: High-reaching High"-reach`ing (?), a. Reaching high or upward; hence, ambitious; aspiring. Shak.

highred.c: High-red High"-red` (?), a. Of a strong red color.

highroad.c: Highroad High"road` (?), n. A highway; a much traveled or main road. [Mostly British]

highseasoned.c: High-seasoned High"-sea`soned (?), a. Enriched with spice and condiments; hence, exciting; piquant.

highsighted.c: High-sighted High"-sight`ed (?), a. Looking upward; supercilious. Shak.

highsouled.c: High-souled High"-souled` (?), a. Having a high or noble spirit; honorable. E. Everett.

highsounding.c: High-sounding High"-sound`ing (?), a. Pompous; noisy; ostentatious; as, high-sounding words or titles.

highspirited.c: High-spirited High"-spir`it*ed (?), a. Full of spirit or natural fire; haughty; courageous; impetuous; not brooking restraint or opposition.

highstepper.c: High-stepper High"-step`per (?), n. A horse that moves with a high step or proud gait; hence, a person having a proud bearing. [Colloq.]

highstomached.c: High-stomached High"-stom`ached (?), a. Having a lofty spirit; haughty. [Obs.] Shak.

highstrung.c: High-strung High"-strung` (?), a. Strung to a high pitch; spirited; sensitive; as, a high-strung horse.

hight.c: Hight Hight (?), n. A variant of Height.

Hight Hight (?), v. t. & i. [imp. Hight, Hot (?), p. p. Hight, Hote (?), Hoten (?). See Hote.] [OE. heiten, highten, haten, hoten; also hight, hatte, hette, is called, was called, AS. hātan to call, name, be called, to command, promise; also hātte is called, was called; akin to G. heissen to call, be called, bid, Goth. haitan to call, in the passive, to be called.] 1. To be called or named. [Archaic & Poetic.]

highth.c: Highth Highth (hīth or hītth), n. Variant of Height. [Obs.]

hightoned.c: High-toned High"-toned` (?), a. 1. High in tone or sound.

hightop.c: High-top High"-top` (?), n. A ship's masthead. Shak.

highway.c: Highway High"way` (?), n. A road or way open to the use of the public, especially a paved main road or thoroughfare between towns; in the latter sense it contrasts with local street; as, on the highways and byways.

highwayman.c: Highwayman High"way`man (?), n.; pl. Highwaymen (?). One who robs on the public road; a highway robber.

highwrought.c: High-wrought High"-wrought` (?), a. 1. Wrought with fine art or skill; elaborate. [Obs.] Pope.

higtaper.c: Hig-taper Hig"-ta`per (?), n. [Cf. Hag-taper.] (Bot.) A plant of the genus Verbascum (Verbascum Thapsus); the common mullein. [Also high-taper and hag-taper.]

hijra.c: Hijra Hijera Hij"e*ra (?), Hij"ra (?), n. See Hegira.

hike.c: Hike Hike (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hiked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hiking.] [Cf. Hitch.] 1. To move with a swing, toss, throw, jerk, or the like. [Dial. or Colloq.]
Hike Hike (?), v. i. 1. To hike one's self; specif., to go with exertion or effort; to tramp; to march laboriously. [Dial. or Colloq.] “If you persist in heaving and hiking like this.” Kipling.
Hike Hike, n. 1. The act of hiking.

hilal.c: Hilal Hi"lal (?), a. Of or pertaining to a hilum.

hilar.c: Hilar Hi"lar (?), a. (Bot.) Belonging to the hilum.

hilarious.c: Hilarious Hi*la"ri*ous (?), a. [L. hilaris, hilarus, Gr.?; cf.? gracious, kindly.] Mirthful; noisy; merry.

hilarity.c: Hilarity Hi*lar"i*ty (?; 277), n. [L. hilaritas: cf. F. hilarité. See Hilarious.] Boisterous mirth; merriment; jollity. Goldsmith.

hilary.c: Hilary term Hil"a*ry term` (?). Formerly, one of the four terms of the courts of common law in England, beginning on the eleventh of January and ending on the thirty-first of the same month, in each year; -- so called from the festival of St. Hilary, January 13th.

hilding.c: Hilding Hil"ding (?), n. [Prob. a corruption of hindling, dim. of hind, adj. Cf. Prov. E. hilderling, hinderling. See Hinderling.] A base, menial wretch. -- a. Base; spiritless. [Obs.] Shak.

hile.c: Hile Hile (?), v. t. To hide. See Hele. [Obs.] Chaucer.

hill.c: Hill Hill (?), n. [OE. hil, hul, AS. hyll; akin to OD. hille, hil, L. collis, and prob. to E. haulm, holm, and column. Cf. 2d Holm.] 1. A natural elevation of land, or a mass of earth rising above the common level of the surrounding land; an eminence less than a mountain.
Hill Hill (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hilled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hilling.] To surround with earth; to heap or draw earth around or upon; as, to hill corn.

hilliness.c: Hilliness Hill"i*ness (?), n. The state of being hilly.

hilling.c: Hilling Hill"ing, n. The act or process of heaping or drawing earth around plants.

hillock.c: Hillock Hill"ock (?), n. A small hill. Shak.

hillside.c: Hillside Hill"side` (?), n. The side or declivity of a hill.

hilltop.c: Hilltop Hill"top` (?), n. The top of a hill.

hilly.c: Hilly Hill"y (?), a. 1. Abounding with hills; uneven in surface; as, a hilly country. “Hilly steep.” Dryden.

hilt.c: Hilt Hilt (?), n. [AS. hilt, hilte; akin to OHG. helza, Prov. G. hilze, Icel. hjalt.] 1. A handle; especially, the handle of a sword, dagger, or the like.

hilted.c: Hilted Hilt"ed, a. Having a hilt; -- used in composition; as, basket-hilted, cross-hilted.

hilum.c: Hilum Hi"lum (?), n. [L., a little thing, trifle.] 1. (Bot.) The eye of a bean or other seed; the mark or scar at the point of attachment of an ovule or seed to its base or support; -- called also hile.

him.c: Him Him (hĭm), pron. Them. See Hem. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Him Him, pron. [AS. him, dat. of hē. √183. See He.] The objective case of he. See He.

himalayan.c: Himalayan Hi*ma"la*yan (?), a. [Skr. himālaya, prop., the abode of snow.] Of or pertaining to the Himalayas, the great mountain chain in Asia.

himself.c: Himself Him*self" (?), pron. 1. An emphasized form of the third person masculine pronoun; -- used as a subject usually with he; as, he himself will bear the blame; used alone in the predicate, either in the nominative or objective case; as, it is himself who saved himself.

himselven.c: Himselven Himselve Himself Him*self" (?), Him*selve" (?), Him*selv"en (?), pron. pl. Themselves. See Hemself. [Obs.] Chaucer.

himyaritic.c: Himyaritic Himyaric { Him*yar"ic (?), Him`ya*rit"ic (?), } a. Pertaining to Himyar, an ancient king of Yemen, in Arabia, or to his successors or people; as, the Himjaritic characters, language, etc.; applied esp. to certain ancient inscriptions showing the primitive type of the oldest form of the Arabic, still spoken in Southern Arabia. Brande & C.

hin.c: Hin Hin (hĭn), n. [Heb. hīn.] A Hebrew measure of liquids, containing three quarts, one pint, one gill, English measure. W. H. Ward.

hind.c: Hind Hind (hīnd), n. [AS. hind; akin to D. hinde, OHG. hinta, G. hinde, hindin, Icel., Sw., & Dan. hind, and perh. to Goth. hinþan to seize (in comp.), E. hunt, or cf. Gr. kema`s a young deer.] 1. (Zool.) The female of the red deer, of which the male is the stag.

Hind Hind, n. [OE. hine, AS. hīne, hīna, orig. gen. pl. of hīwan domestics; akin to Icel. hjū man and wife, domestics, family, Goth. heiwafrauja master of the house, G. heirath marriage; cf. L. civis citizen, E. city or E. home. Cf. Hide a measure of land.] 1. A domestic; a servant. [Obs.] Shak.

Hind Hind, a. [Compar. Hinder (?); superl. Hindmost (?), or Hindermost (?).] [OE. hind, adv., back, AS. hindan behind. See Hinder, a.] In the rear; -- opposed to front; of or pertaining to the part or end which follows or is behind, in opposition to the part which leads or is before; as, the hind legs or hind feet of a quadruped; the hind man in a procession.

hindberry.c: Hindberry Hind"ber*ry (?), n. [AS. hindberie; akin to OHG. hintberi, G. himbeere. So called because hinds or stags are fond of them. See 1st Hind, and Berry.] The raspberry. [Prov. Eng.]

hindbrain.c: Hindbrain Hind"brain` (?), n. [Hind, adj. + brain.] (Anat.) The posterior of the three principal divisions of the brain, including the epencephalon and metencephalon. Sometimes restricted to the epencephalon only.

hinder.c: Hinder Hind"er (?), a. [OE. hindere, AS. hinder, adv., behind; akin to OHG. hintar, prep., behind, G. hinter, Goth. hindar; orig. a comparative, and akin to AS. hine hence. See Hence, He, and cf. Hind, a., Hindmost.] Of or belonging to that part or end which is in the rear, or which follows; as, the hinder part of a wagon; the hinder parts of a horse.

Hinder Hin"der (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hindered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hindering.] [OE. hindren, hinderen, AS. hindrian, fr. hinder behind; akin to D. hinderen, G. hindern, OHG. hintar?n, Icel. & Sw. hindra, Dan. hindre. See Hinder, a.] 1. To keep back or behind; to prevent from starting or moving forward; to check; to retard; to obstruct; to bring to a full stop; -- often followed by from; as, an accident hindered the coach; drought hinders the growth of plants; to hinder me from going.
Hinder Hin"der, v. i. To interpose obstacles or impediments; to be a hindrance.

hinderer.c: Hinderer Hin"der*er (?), n. One who, or that which, hinders.

hinderest.c: Hinderest Hind"er*est (?), a. Hindermost; -- superl. of Hind, a. [Obs.] Chaucer.

hinderling.c: Hinderling Hind"er*ling (?), n. [AS. hinderling one who comes behind his ancestors, fr. AS. hinder behind. See Hinder, a., and cf. Hilding.] A worthless, base, degenerate person or animal. [Obs.] Callander.

hindmost.c: Hindmost Hindermost { Hind"er*most`, Hind"most` } (?), a. [The superlative of hind. See Hind, a.] [Cf. AS. hindema (akin to Goth. hindumists), a superlative from the same source as the comparative hinder. See Hinder, a., and cf. Aftermost.] Furthest in or toward the rear; last. “Rachel and Joseph hindermost.” Gen. xxxiii. 2.

hindgut.c: Hindgut Hind"gut` (?), n. [Hind, a. + gut.] (Anat.) The posterior part of the alimentary canal, including the rectum, and sometimes the large intestine also.

hindi.c: Hindi Hin"di (?), n. [Prop. a Per. adj. meaning, Indian, Hindoo.] The name given by Europeans to that form of the Hindustani language which is chiefly spoken by native Hindus. In employs the Devanagari character, in which Sanskrit is written. Whitworth.

hindleys.c: Hindleys screw Hind"ley"s screw` (?). (Mech.) A screw cut on a solid whose sides are arcs of the periphery of a wheel into the teeth of which the screw is intended to work. It is named from the person who first used the form.

hindu.c: Hindu Hindoo { Hin"doo, Hin"du } (?; 277), n.; pl. Hindoos (#) or Hindus. [Per. Hindū, fr. Hind, Hindūstān, India. Cf. Indian.] A native inhabitant of Hindostan. As an ethnical term it is confined to the Dravidian and Aryan races; as a religious name it is restricted to followers of the Veda.

Hindu calendar Hindoo calendar {Hin"doo calendar or Hindu calendar }. A lunisolar calendar of India, according to which the year is divided into twelve months, with an extra month inserted after every month in which two new moons occur (once in three years). The intercalary month has the name of the one which precedes it. The year usually commences about April 11. The months are follows:
Hindu Hin"du (?), n. Same as Hindoo. This is now the more commonly used spelling.

hinduism.c: Hinduism Hindooism { Hin"doo*ism, Hin"du*ism } (?), n. The religious doctrines and rites of the Hindus; Brahmanism.

hindustani.c: Hindustani Hindoostani Hindoostanee { Hin"doo*sta"nee, Hin"doo*sta"ni, Hin"du*sta"ni } (?), a. [Hind. Hindūstānī an Indian, fr. Hind. and Per. Hindūstān India.] Of or pertaining to the Hindoos or their language. -- n. The language of Hindustan; the name given by Europeans to the most generally spoken of the modern Aryan languages of India. It is Hindi with the addition of Persian and Arabic words.

hindrance.c: Hindrance Hin"drance (?), n. [See Hinder, v. t.] 1. The act of hindering, or the state of being hindered.

hine.c: Hine Hine (?), n. [See Hind a servant.] A servant; a farm laborer; a peasant; a hind. [Obs.]

hinge.c: Hinge Hinge (?), n. [OE. henge, heeng; akin to D. heng, LG. henge, Prov. E. hingle a small hinge; connected with hang, v., and Icel. hengja to hang. See Hang.]
Hinge Hinge, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hinged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hinging (?).] 1. To attach by, or furnish with, hinges.

Hinge Hinge (?), v. i. To stand, depend, hang, or turn, as on a hinge; to depend chiefly for a result or decision or for force and validity; -- usually with on or upon; as, the argument hinges on this point. I. Taylor

hingeless.c: Hingeless Hinge"less (?), a. Without a hinge or joint.

hink.c: Hink Hink (?), n. A reaping hook. Knight.

hinny.c: Hinny Hinniate { Hin"ni*ate (?), Hin"ny (?) } v. i. [L. hinnire.] To neigh; to whinny. [Obs.]
Hinny Hin"ny, n.; pl. Hinnies (#). [L. hinnus, cf. Gr.?.] A hybrid between a stallion and an ass; -- correlative of the mule.
Hinny Hin"ny, n. A term of endearment; darling; -- corrupted from honey. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.

hint.c: Hint Hint (hĭnt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hinted; p. pr. & vb. n. Hinting.] [OE. henten, hinten, to seize, to catch, AS. hentan to pursue, take, seize; or Icel. ymta to mutter, ymtr a muttering, Dan. ymte to whisper. √36. Cf. Hent.] To bring to mind by a slight mention or remote allusion; to suggest in an indirect manner; as, to hint a suspicion.
Hint Hint, v. i. To make an indirect reference, suggestion, or allusion; to allude vaguely to something.
Hint Hint, n. A remote allusion; slight mention; intimation; insinuation; a suggestion or reminder, without a full declaration or explanation; also, an occasion or motive.

hinterland.c: hinterland hin"ter*land` (?), n. [G.; hinter behind + land land.] a remote and undeveloped area; originally, the land or region lying behind the coast district. The term is used esp. with reference to the so-called doctrine of the hinterland, sometimes advanced, that occupation of the coast supports a claim to an exclusive right to occupy, from time to time, the territory lying inland of the coast.

hintingly.c: Hintingly Hint"ing*ly (?), adv. In a hinting manner.

hip.c: Hip Hip (?), n. [OE. hipe, huppe, AS. hype; akin to D. heup, OHG. huf, G. hüfte, Dan. hofte, Sw. höft, Goth. hups; cf. Icel. huppr, and also Gr.? the hollow above the hips of cattle, and Lith. kumpis ham.]

Hip Hip, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hipped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hipping.] 1. To dislocate or sprain the hip of, to fracture or injure the hip bone of (a quadruped) in such a manner as to produce a permanent depression of that side.
Hip Hip (?), n. [OE. hepe, AS. heópe; cf. OHG. hiufo a bramble bush.] (Bot.) The fruit of a rosebush, especially of the English dog-rose (Rosa canina); called also rose hip. [Written also hop, hep.]
Hip Hip, interj. Used to excite attention or as a signal; as, hip, hip, hurra!
Hip lock Hip lock. (Wrestling) A lock in which a close grip is obtained and a fall attempted by a heave over the hip.

hipps.c: Hipps Hip Hip, or Hipps (?), n. See Hyp, n. [Colloq.]

hype.c: Hype Hipe {Hipe (?), n. Also Hype }. [Etym. uncertain.] (Wrestling) A throw in which the wrestler lifts his opponent from the ground, swings him to one side, knocks up his nearer thigh from the back with the knee, and throws him on his back.

hipe.c: Hipe Hipe, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Hiped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hiping (?).] (Wrestling) To throw by means of a hipe. -- Hip"er (#), n.

hiphalt.c: Hiphalt Hip"halt` (?), a. Lame in the hip. [R.] Gower.

hippe.c: Hippe Hippa { Hip"pa (?), Hip"pe (?), } n. (Zool.) A genus of marine decapod crustaceans, which burrow rapidly in the sand by pushing themselves backward; -- called also bait bug. See Illust. under Anomura.

hipparion.c: Hipparion ‖Hip*pa"ri*on (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a pony, dim. of? a horse.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of Tertiary mammals allied to the horse, but three-toed, having on each foot a small lateral hoof on each side of the main central one. It is believed to be one of the ancestral genera of the Horse family.

hippish.c: Hippish Hipped { Hipped (?), Hip"pish (?), } a. [From 5th Hip.] Somewhat hypochondriac; melancholy. See Hyppish. [Colloq.]

hippobosca.c: Hippobosca ‖Hip`po*bos"ca (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. "i`ppos horse +? to feed.] (Zool.) A genus of dipterous insects including the horsefly or horse tick. -- Hip`po*bos"can (#), a.

hippocampal.c: Hippocampal Hip`po*cam"pal (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the hippocampus.

hippocampus.c: Hippocampus Hip`po*cam"pus (?), n. [L., the sea horse, Gr.? a hippocampus (in senses 1 and 2); "i`ppos horse +? to bend.] 1. (Class. Myth.) A fabulous monster, with the head and fore quarters of a horse joined to the tail of a dolphin or other fish (Hippocampus brevirostris), -- seen in Pompeian paintings, attached to the chariot of Neptune. Fairholt.

hippocentaur.c: Hippocentaur Hip`po*cen"taur (?), n. [L. hippocentaurus, Gr.?; "i`ppos horse +? centaur.] (Myth.) Same as Centaur.

hippocras.c: Hippocras Hip"po*cras (?), n. [F. hippocras, hypocras, NL. vinum hippocraticum, lit., wine of Hippocrates.] A cordial made of spiced wine, etc.

hippocrates.c: Hippocrates Hip*poc"ra*tes (?), n. A famous Greek physician and medical writer, born in Cos, about 460 b. c.

hippocratic.c: Hippocratic Hip"po*crat"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to Hippocrates, or to his teachings.

hippocratism.c: Hippocratism Hip*poc"ra*tism (?), n. The medical philosophy or system of Hippocrates.

hippocrene.c: Hippocrene Hip"po*crene (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?; "i`ppos horse +? a fountain.] A fountain on Mount Helicon in Bœotia, fabled to have burst forth when the ground was struck by the hoof of Pegasus. Also, its waters, which were supposed to impart poetic inspiration. Keats.

hippocrepian.c: Hippocrepian Hip"po*crep"i*an (?), n. [See Hippocrepiform.] (Zool.) One of an order of fresh-water Bryozoa, in which the tentacles are on a lophophore, shaped like a horseshoe. See Phylactolæma.

hippocrepiform.c: Hippocrepiform Hip`po*crep`i*form (?), a. [Gr. "i`ppos horse +? shoe + -form.] (Bot.) Shaped like a horseshoe.

hippodame.c: Hippodame Hip"po*dame (?), n. [Cf. F. hippopotame.] A fabulous sea monster. [Obs.] Spenser.

hippodrome.c: Hippodrome Hip"po*drome (?), n. [L. hippodromos, Gr.?; "i`ppos horse +? course, fr.? to run: cf. F. hippodrome.] 1. (Gr. Antiq.) A place set apart for equestrian and chariot races.
Hippodrome Hip"po*drome, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Hippodromed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hippodroming.] (Sports) To arrange contests with predetermined winners. [Slang, U. S.]

hippogriff.c: Hippogriff Hip"po*griff (?), n. [F. hippogriffe; cf. It. ippogrifo. See Hippopotamus, Griffon.] (Myth.) A fabulous winged animal, half horse and half griffin. Milton.

hippolith.c: Hippolith Hip"po*lith (?), n. [Gr. "i`ppos horse + -lith.] A concretion, or kind of bezoar, from the intestines of the horse.

hippopathology.c: Hippopathology Hip`po*pa*thol`o*gy (?), n. [Gr. "i`ppos horse + E. pathology: cf. F. hippopathologie.] The science of veterinary medicine; the pathology of the horse.

hippophagi.c: Hippophagi Hip*poph"a*gi (?), n. pl. [NL. See Hippophagous.] Eaters of horseflesh.

hippophagist.c: Hippophagist Hip*poph"a*gist (?), n. One who eats horseflesh.

hippophagous.c: Hippophagous Hip*poph"a*gous (?), a. [Gr. "i`ppos horse +? to eat: cf. F. hippophage.] Feeding on horseflesh; -- said of certain nomadic tribes, as the Tartars.

hippophagy.c: Hippophagy Hip*poph"a*gy (?), n. [Cf. F. hippophagie.] The act or practice of feeding on horseflesh.

hippophile.c: Hippophile Hip"po*phile (?), n. [Gr. "i`ppos horse +? to love.] One who loves horses. Holmes.

hippopotamus.c: Hippopotamus Hip`po*pot"a*mus (?), n.; pl. E. Hippopotamuses (#), L. Hippopotami (#). [L., from Gr.?; "i`ppos horse +? river. Cf. Equine.] (Zool.) A large, amphibious, herbivorous mammal (Hippopotamus amphibius), common in the rivers of tropical Africa. It is allied to the hogs, and has a very thick, naked skin, a thick and square head, a very large muzzle, small eyes and ears, thick and heavy body, and short legs. It is supposed to be the behemoth of the Bible. Called also zeekoe, and river horse. A smaller species (Hippopotamus Liberiencis) inhabits Western Africa.

hippotomy.c: Hippotomy Hip*pot"o*my (?), n. [Gr. "i`ppos horse +? to cut: cf. F. hippotomie.] Anatomy of the horse.

hippuric.c: Hippuric Hip*pu"ric (?), a. [Gr. "i`ppos horse + o"y`ron urine: cf. F. hippurique.] (Physiol. Chem.) Obtained from the urine of horses; as, hippuric acid.

hippurite.c: Hippurite Hip"pu*rite (?), n. [Gr.? decked with a horse's tail; "i`ppos horse +? tail: cf. F. hippurite.] (Paleon.) A fossil bivalve mollusk of the genus Hippurites, of many species, having a conical, cup-shaped under valve, with a flattish upper valve or lid. Hippurites are found only in the Cretaceous rocks.

hiproofed.c: Hip-roofed Hip"-roofed` (?), a. Having a hip roof.

hipshot.c: Hipshot Hip"shot` (?), a. [Hip + shot.] Having the hip dislocated; hence, having one hip lower than the other. L'Estrange.

hir.c: Hir Hir (?), pron. [Obs.] See Here, pron. Chaucer.

hircic.c: Hircic Hir"cic (?), a. [Cf. F. hircique. See Hircin.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or derived from, mutton suet; -- applied by Chevreul to an oily acid which was obtained from mutton suet, and to which he attributed the peculiar taste and smell of that substance. The substance has also been called hircin. Watts.

hircin.c: Hircin Hir"cin (?), n. [L. hircus, he-goat, buck: cf. F. hircine.] (Chem.) Hircic acid. See Hircic. [R.]

hircinous.c: Hircinous Hircine { Hir"cine (?), Hir"ci*nous (?), } a. [L. hircinus, fr. hircus hegoat: cf. F. hircin.] 1. Goatlike; of or pertaining to a goat or the goats.

hire.c: Hire Hire (hẽr), pron. [Obs.] See Here, pron. Chaucer.

Hire Hire (hīr), n. [OE. hire, hure, AS. hȳr; akin to D. huur, G. heuer, Dan. hyre, Sw. hyra.] 1. The price, reward, or compensation paid, or contracted to be paid, for the temporary use of a thing or a place, for personal service, or for labor; wages; rent; pay.
Hire Hire, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hired (hīrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Hiring.] [OE. hiren, huren, AS. hȳrian; akin to D. huren, G. heuern, Dan. hyre, Sw. hyra. See Hire, n.]

Hire and purchase agreement Hire purchase agreement Hire purchase { Hire purchase, or, more fully, Hire purchase agreement, or Hire and purchase agreement}. (Law) A contract (more fully called contract of hire with an option of purchase) in which a person hires goods for a specified period and at a fixed rent, with the added condition that if he shall retain the goods for the full period and pay all the installments of rent as they become due the contract shall determine and the title vest absolutely in him, and that if he chooses he may at any time during the term surrender the goods and be quit of any liability for future installments upon the contract. In the United States such a contract is generally treated as a conditional sale, and the term hire purchase is also sometimes applied to a contract in which the hirer is not free to avoid future liability by surrender of the goods. In England, however, if the hirer does not have this right the contract is a sale.

hireling.c: Hireling Hire"ling (hīr"lĭng), n. [AS. hȳreling. See Hire, n., and -ling.] One who is hired, or who serves for wages; esp., one whose motive and interest in serving another are wholly gainful; a mercenary. “Lewd hirelings.” Milton.
Hireling Hire"ling, a. Serving for hire or wages; venal; mercenary. “Hireling mourners.” Dryden.

hirs.c: Hirs Hires Hires (?), Hirs, pron. Hers; theirs. See Here, pron. [Obs.] Chaucer.

hirsute.c: Hirsute Hir*sute" (?), a. [L. hirsutus; prob. akin to horridus horrid. Cf. Horrid.] 1. Rough with hair; set with bristles; shaggy.

hirtellous.c: Hirtellous Hir*tel"lous (?), a. [Dim., fr. L. hirtus hairy.] (Bot. & Zool.) Pubescent with minute and somewhat rigid hairs.

hirudine.c: Hirudine Hi*ru"dine (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the leeches.

hirudinea.c: Hirudinea ‖Hir`u*din"e*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. hirudo, hirudinis, a leech.] (Zool.) An order of Annelida, including the leeches; -- called also Hirudinei.

hirudo.c: Hirudo ‖Hi*ru"do (?), n. [L., a leech.] (Zool.) A genus of leeches, including the common medicinal leech. See Leech.

hirundine.c: Hirundine Hi*run"dine (?), a. (Zool.) Like or pertaining to the swallows.

hirundo.c: Hirundo ‖Hi*run"do (?), n. [L., swallow.] (Zool.) A genus of birds including the swallows and martins.

his.c: His His (hĭz), pron. [AS. his of him, his, gen. masc. & neut. of hē, neut. hit. See He.] 1. Belonging or pertaining to him; -- used as a pronominal adjective or adjective pronoun; as, tell John his papers are ready; formerly used also for its, but this use is now obsolete.

hisingerite.c: Hisingerite His"ing*er*ite (?), n. [Named after W. Hisinger, a Swedish mineralogist.] (Min.) A soft black, iron ore, nearly earthy, a hydrous silicate of iron.

hispanic.c: Hispanic His*pan"ic (?), a. [L. Hispanicus.] Of or pertaining to Spain or its language; as, Hispanic words.

hispanicism.c: Hispanicism His*pan"i*cism, n. A Spanish idiom or mode of speech. Keightley.

hispanicize.c: Hispanicize His*pan"i*cize (?), v. t. To give a Spanish form or character to; as, to Hispanicize Latin words.

hispid.c: Hispid His"pid (?), a. [L. hispidus: cf. F. hispide.]

hispidulous.c: Hispidulous His*pid"u*lous (?), a. [Dim. of hispid.] (Bot. & Zool.) Minutely hispid.

hiss.c: Hiss Hiss (hĭs). v. i. [imp. & p. p. Hissed (hĭst); p. pr. & vb. n. Hissing.] [AS. hysian; prob. of imitative origin; cf. LG. hissen, OD. hisschen.] 1. To make with the mouth a prolonged sound like that of the letter s, by driving the breath between the tongue and the teeth; to make with the mouth a sound like that made by a goose or a snake when angered; esp., to make such a sound as an expression of hatred, passion, or disapproval.
Hiss Hiss, v. t. 1. To condemn or express contempt for by hissing.
Hiss Hiss, n. 1. A prolonged sound like that letter s, made by forcing out the breath between the tongue and teeth, esp. as a token of disapprobation or contempt.

hissing.c: Hissing Hiss"ing, n. 1. The act of emitting a hiss or hisses.

hissingly.c: Hissingly Hiss"ing*ly, adv. With a hissing sound.

hist.c: Hist Hist (?), interj. [Cf. Dan. hys.?. Cf. Hush, Whist.] Hush; be silent; -- a signal for silence. Milton.

histiology.c: Histiology His`ti*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. "isto`s tissue + -logy.] Same as Histology.

histogenesis.c: Histogenesis His`to*gen"e*sis (?), n. [Gr. "isto`s tissue + E. genesis.] (Biol.) (a) The formation and development of organic tissues; histogeny; -- the opposite of histolysis. (b) Germ history of cells, and of the tissues composed of cells. Haeckel.

histogenetic.c: Histogenetic His`to*ge*net"ic (?), a. [See Histogeny.] (Biol.) Tissue-producing; connected with the formation and development of the organic tissues.

histogeny.c: Histogeny His*tog"e*ny (?), n. [Gr. "isto`s tissue + root of gi`gnesqai to be born.] (Biol.) Same as Histogenesis. Dunglison.

histographer.c: Histographer His*tog"ra*pher (?), n. One who describes organic tissues; an histologist.

histographical.c: Histographical His"to*graph"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to histography.

histography.c: Histography His*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. "isto`s tissue + -graphy.] A description of, or treatise on, organic tissues.

histohaematin.c: Histohaematin His`to*hæm"a*tin (?), n. [Gr. "isto`s tissue + E. hæmatin.] (Physiol.) One of a class of respiratory pigments, widely distributed in the animal kingdom, capable of ready oxidation and reduction.

histoid.c: Histoid His"toid (?), a. [Gr. "isto`s tissue + -oid.] Resembling the normal tissues; as, histoid tumors.

histological.c: Histological Histologic { His`to*log"ic (?), His`to*log"ic*al } a. (Biol.) Pertaining to histology, or to the microscopic structure of the tissues of living organisms. -- His`to*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

histologist.c: Histologist His*tol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in histology.

histology.c: Histology His*tol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. "isto`s tissue + -logy.] That branch of biological science, which treats of the minute (microscopic) structure of animal and vegetable tissues; -- called also histiology.

histolysis.c: Histolysis ‖His*tol"y*sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. "isto`s tissue +? to loosen, dissolve.] (Biol.) The decay and dissolution of the organic tissues and of the blood.

histolytic.c: Histolytic His`to*lyt"ic (?), a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to histolysis, or the degeneration of tissues.

histonomy.c: Histonomy His*ton"o*my (?), n. [Gr. "isto`s tissue +? to distribute, regulate.] The science which treats of the laws relating to organic tissues, their formation, development, functions, etc.

histophyly.c: Histophyly His*toph"y*ly (?), n. [Gr. "isto`s tissue + Gr.? clan.] (Biol.) The tribal history of cells, a division of morphophyly. Haeckel.

historial.c: Historial His*to"ri*al (?), a. [L. historialis: cf. F. historial.] Historical. [Obs.] Chaucer.

historian.c: Historian His*to"ri*an (?), n. [F. historien.] 1. A writer of history; a chronicler; an annalist.

historical.c: historical historic { his*tor"ic (hĭs*tŏr"ĭk), his*tor"ic*al (hĭs*tŏr"ĭ*kail), } a. [L. historicus, Gr. "istoriko`s: cf. F. historique. See History.] Of or pertaining to history, or the record of past events; as, an historical poem; the historic page. -- His*tor"ic*al*ness, n. -- His*to*ric"i*ty (#), n.

historically.c: Historically His*tor"ic*al*ly (?), adv. In the manner of, or in accordance with, history.

historicize.c: Historicize His*tor"i*cize (?), v. t. To record or narrate in the manner of a history; to chronicle. [R.]

historiette.c: Historiette ‖His`to*ri*ette" (?), n. [F., dim. of histoire a history.] Historical narration on a small scale; a brief recital; a story. Emerson.

historify.c: Historify His*tor"i*fy (?), v. t. [History + -fy.] To record in or as history. [R.] Lamb.

historiographer.c: Historiographer His*to`ri*og"ra*pher (hĭs*tō`rĭ*ŏg"rȧ*fẽr), n. [L. historiographus, Gr. "istoriogra`fos; "istori`a history + gra`fein to write: cf. F. historiographe.] An historian; a writer of history; especially, one appointed or designated to write a history; also, a title bestowed by some governments upon historians of distinction.

historiographership.c: Historiographership His*to`ri*og"ra*pher*ship, n. The office of an historiographer. Saintsbury.

historiography.c: Historiography His*to`ri*og"ra*phy (?), n. The art of employment of an historiographer.

historiology.c: Historiology His*to`ri*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? history + -logy.] A discourse on history. Cockeram.

historionomer.c: Historionomer His*to`ri*on"o*mer (?), n. [Gr.? history +? to distribute.] One versed in the phenomena of history and the laws controlling them.

historize.c: Historize His"to*rize (?), v. t. To relate as history; to chronicle; to historicize. [R.] Evelyn.

history.c: History His"to*ry (?), n.; pl. Histories (#). [L. historia, Gr. 'istori`a history, information, inquiry, fr. 'istwr, "istwr, knowing, learned, from the root of? to know; akin to E. wit. See Wit, and cf. Story.]
History His"to*ry, v. t. To narrate or record. [Obs.] Shak.

histotomy.c: Histotomy His*tot"o*my (?), n. [Gr.? tissue +? to cut.] The dissection of organic tissues.

histozyme.c: Histozyme His"to*zyme (?), n. [Gr.? tissue +? leaven.] (Physiol. Chem.) A soluble enzyme occurring in the animal body, to the presence of which many normal decompositions and synthetical processes are supposed to be due.

histrion.c: Histrion His"tri*on (?), n. [L. histrio: cf. F. histrion.] A player. [R.] Pope.

histrionical.c: Histrionical Histrionic { His`tri*on"ic (?), His`tri*on"ic*al (?) }, a. [L. histrionicus: cf. F. histrionique. See Histrion.] 1. Of or relating to the stage or a stageplayer; befitting a theatre; theatrical.

histrionicism.c: Histrionicism His`tri*on"i*cism (?), n. The histrionic art; stageplaying. W. Black.

histrionism.c: Histrionism His"tri*o*nism (?), n. Theatrical representation; acting; affectation. Sir T. Browne.

histrionize.c: Histrionize His"tri*o*nize (?), v. t. To act; to represent on the stage, or theatrically. Urquhart.

hit.c: Hit Hit, 3d pers. sing. pres. of Hide, contracted from hideth. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Hit Hit (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hit; p. pr. & vb. n. Hitting.] [OE. hitten, hutten, of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. hitte to hit, find, Sw. & Icel. hitta.] 1. To reach with a stroke or blow; to strike or touch, usually with force; especially, to reach or touch (an object aimed at).
Hit Hit (?), v. i. 1. To meet or come in contact; to strike; to clash; -- followed by against or on.
Hit Hit, n. 1. A striking against; the collision of one body against another; the stroke that touches anything.

hitch.c: Hitch Hitch (hĭch), v. t. [Cf. Scot. hitch a motion by a jerk, and hatch, hotch, to move by jerks, also Prov. G. hiksen, G. hinken, to limp, hobble; or E. hiccough; or possibly akin to E. hook.] 1. To become entangled or caught; to be linked or yoked; to unite; to cling.

Hitch Hitch, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hitched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hitching.] 1. To hook; to catch or fasten as by a hook or a knot; to make fast, unite, or yoke; as, to hitch a horse, or a halter; hitch your wagon to a star.
Hitch Hitch, n. 1. A catch; anything that holds, as a hook; an impediment; an obstacle; an entanglement.

hitchel.c: Hitchel Hitch"el (?), n. & v. t. See Hatchel.

hithe.c: Hithe Hithe (hīth), n. [AS. hȳð. Cf. Hide to conceal.] A port or small haven; -- used in composition; as, Lambhithe, now Lambeth. Pennant.

hither.c: Hither Hith"er (?), adv. [OE. hider, AS. hider; akin to Icel. hēðra, Dan. hid, Sw. hit, Goth. hidrē; cf. L. citra on this side, or E. here, he. √183. Cf. He.]
Hither Hith"er, a. 1. Being on the side next or toward the person speaking; nearer; -- correlate of thither and farther; as, on the hither side of a hill. Milton.

hithermost.c: Hithermost Hith"er*most` (?), a. Nearest on this side. Sir M. Hale.

hitherto.c: Hitherto Hith"er*to` (?), adv. 1. To this place; to a prescribed limit.

hitherward.c: Hitherward Hith"er*ward (?), adv. [AS. hiderweard.] Toward this place; hither.

hitter.c: Hitter Hit"ter (?), n. 1. One who hits or strikes; as, a hard hitter.

hittite.c: Hittite Hit"tite (?), n. [From Heb. Khittīm Hittites.] A member of an ancient people (or perhaps group of peoples) whose settlements extended from Armenia westward into Asia Minor and southward into Palestine. They are known to have been met along the Orontes as early as 1500 b. c., and were often at war with the Egyptians and Assyrians. Especially in the north they developed a considerable civilization, of which numerous monuments and inscriptions are extant. Authorities are not agreed as to their race. While several attempts have been made to decipher the Hittite characters, little progress has yet been made.

hittorf.c: Hittorf rays Hit"torf rays (?). (Elec.) Rays (chiefly cathode rays) developed by the electric discharge in Hittorf tubes.

Hittorf tube Hit"torf tube. (Elec.) (a) A highly exhausted glass tube with metallic electrodes nearly in contact so as to exhibit the insulating effects of a vacuum. It was used by the German physicist W. Hittorf (b. 1824). (b) A Crookes tube.

hive.c: Hive Hive (?), n. [OE. hive, huve, AS. h?fe.] 1. A box, basket, or other structure, for the reception and habitation of a swarm of honeybees. Dryden.
Hive Hive, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hived (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hiving.] 1. To collect into a hive; to place in, or cause to enter, a hive; as, to hive a swarm of bees.
Hive Hive, v. i. To take shelter or lodgings together; to reside in a collective body. Pope.

hiveless.c: Hiveless Hive"less, a. Destitute of a hive. Gascoigne.

hiver.c: Hiver Hiv"er (?), n. One who collects bees into a hive.

hives.c: Hives Hives (?), n. [Scot.; perh. akin to E. heave.] (Med.) (a) The croup. (b) An eruptive disease (Varicella globularis), allied to the chicken pox.

hizz.c: Hizz Hizz (?), v. i. To hiss. [Obs.] Shak.

hoa.c: Hoa Ho { Ho, Hoa } (?), n. [See Ho, interj., 2.] A stop; a halt; a moderation of pace.
Hoa Ho { Ho, Hoa } (hō), interj. [Cf. F. & G. ho.] 1. Halloo! attend! -- a call to excite attention, or to give notice of approach. “What noise there, ho?” Shak. “Ho! who's within?” Shak.

hoar.c: Hoar Hoar (?), a. [OE. hor, har, AS. hār; akin to Icel. hārr, and to OHG. hēr illustrious, magnificent; cf. Icel. Heið brightness of the sky, Goth. hais torch, Skr. kētus light, torch. Cf. Hoary.] 1. White, or grayish white; as, hoar frost; hoar cliffs. “Hoar waters.” Spenser.
Hoar Hoar, v. t. [AS. hārian to grow gray.] To become moldy or musty. [Obs.] Shak.

hoard.c: Hoard Hoard, n. [OE. hord, AS. hord; akin to OS. hord, G. hort, Icel. hodd, Goth. huzd; prob. from the root of E. hide to conceal, and of L. custos guard, E. custody. See Hide to conceal.] A store, stock, or quantity of anything accumulated or laid up; a hidden supply; a treasure; as, a hoard of provisions; a hoard of money.

Hoard Hoard, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hoarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Hoarding.] [AS. hordian.] To collect and lay up; to amass and deposit in secret; to store secretly, or for the sake of keeping and accumulating; as, to hoard grain.
Hoard Hoard, v. i. To lay up a store or hoard, as of money.

hoarding.c: Hoarding Hoard"ing (?), n. [From OF. hourd, hourt, barrier, palisade, of German or Dutch origin; cf. D. horde hurdle, fence, G. horde, hürde; akin to E. hurdle. √16. See Hurdle.] 1. (Arch.) A screen of boards inclosing a house and materials while builders are at work. [Eng.]

hoarfrost.c: Hoarfrost Hoar"frost` (?), n. The white particles formed by the congelation of dew; white frost. [Written also horefrost. See Hoar, a.]

hoariness.c: Hoariness Hoar"i*ness (?), n. [From Hoary.] The state of being hoary. Dryden.

hoarse.c: Hoarse Hoarse (?), a. [Compar. Hoarser (?), superl. Hoarsest.] [OE. hors, also hos, has, AS. hās; akin to D. heesch, G. heiser, Icel. hāss, Dan. hæs, Sw. hes. Cf. Prov. E. heazy.] 1. Having a harsh, rough, grating voice or sound, as when affected with a cold; making a rough, harsh cry or sound; as, the hoarse raven.

hoarsely.c: Hoarsely Hoarse"ly, adv. With a harsh, grating sound or voice.

hoarsen.c: Hoarsen Hoars"en (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hoarsened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hoarsening.] To make hoarse.

hoarseness.c: Hoarseness Hoarse"ness (?), n. Harshness or roughness of voice or sound, due to mucus collected on the vocal cords, or to swelling or looseness of the cords.

hoarstone.c: Hoarstone Hoar"stone` (hōr"stōn`), n. A stone designating the bounds of an estate; a landmark. Halliwell.

hoary.c: Hoary Hoar"y (?), a. 1. White or whitish. “The hoary willows.” Addison.

hoax.c: Hoax Hoax (?), n. [Prob. contr. fr. hocus, in hocus-pocus.] A deception for mockery or mischief; a deceptive trick or story; a practical joke. Macaulay.
Hoax Hoax, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hoaxed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hoaxing.] To deceive by a story or a trick, for sport or mischief; to impose upon sportively. Lamb.

hoazin.c: Hoazin Hoa"zin (?), n. (Zool.) A remarkable South American bird (Opisthocomus cristatus); the crested touraco. By some Zoologists it is made the type of a distinct order (Opisthocomi).

hob.c: Hob Hob (?), n. [Prob. akin to hump. Cf. Hub. ]
Hob Hob, n. [Orig. an abbrev. of Robin, Robert; Robin Goodfellow a celebrated fairy, or domestic spirit. Cf. Hobgoblin, and see Robin.] 1. A fairy; a sprite; an elf. [Obs.]

hobandnob.c: Hobandnob Hobanob { Hob"a*nob` (?), Hob"and*nob`, } v. i. Same as Hobnob. Tennyson.

hobbism.c: Hobbism Hob"bism (?), n. The philosophical system of Thomas Hobbes, an English materialist (1588-1679); esp., his political theory that the most perfect form of civil government is an absolute monarchy with despotic control over everything relating to law, morals, and religion.

hobbist.c: Hobbist Hob"bist (?), n. One who accepts the doctrines of Thomas Hobbes.

hobble.c: Hobble Hob"ble (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Hobbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hobbling (?).] [OE. hobelen, hoblen, freq. of hoppen to hop; akin to D. hobbelen, hoblen, hoppeln. See Hop to jump, and cf. Hopple ] 1. To walk lame, bearing chiefly on one leg; to walk with a hitch or hop, or with crutches.
Hobble Hob"ble, v. t. 1. To fetter by tying the legs; to hopple; to clog. “ They hobbled their horses.” Dickens
Hobble Hob"ble, n. 1. An unequal gait; a limp; a halt; as, he has a hobble in his gait. Swift.
Hobble skirt Hob"ble skirt. A woman's skirt so scant at the bottom as to restrain freedom of movement after the fashion of a hobble. -- Hob"ble-skirt`ed, a.

hobblebush.c: Hobblebush Hob"ble*bush` (?), n. (Bot.) A low bush (Viburnum lantanoides) having long, straggling branches and handsome flowers. It is found in the Northern United States. Called also shinhopple.

hobbletehoy.c: Hobbletehoy Hobbledehoy { Hob"ble*de*hoy` (?), Hob"ble*te*hoy` (?), } n. [Written also hobbetyhoy, hobbarddehoy, hobbedehoy, hobdehoy.] [ Cf. Prob. E. hobbledygee with a limping movement; also F. hobereau, a country squire, E. hobby, and OF. hoi to-day; perh. the orig. sense was, an upstart of to-day.] A youth between boy and man; an awkward, gawky young fellow. [Colloq.]

hobbler.c: Hobbler Hob"bler, n. [OE. also hobeler, OF. hobelier, LL. hobellarius. See Hobby a horse.] (Eng. Hist.) One who by his tenure was to maintain a horse for military service; a kind of light horseman in the Middle Ages who was mounted on a hobby. Hallam. Sir J. Davies.

hobblingly.c: Hobblingly Hob"bling*ly (?), adv. With a limping step.

hobbly.c: Hobbly Hob"bly (?), a. Rough; uneven; causing one to hobble; as a hobbly road.

hobby.c: Hobby Hob"by (?), n.; pl. Hobbies (#). [OE. hobi; cf. OF. hobe, hobé, F. hobereau a hobby, a species of falcon. OF. hober to move, stir. Cf. Hobby a horse.] (Zool.) A small, strong-winged European falcon (Falco subbuteo), formerly trained for hawking.

hobbyhorse.c: Hobbyhorse Hobby { Hob"by (?), Hob"by*horse` (?), } n. [OE. hobin a nag, OF. hobin hobby; cf. hober to stir, move; prob. of German or Scand. origin; cf. Dan. hoppe a mare, dial. Sw. hoppa; perh. akin to E. hop to jump.] 1. A strong, active horse, of a middle size, said to have been originally from Ireland; an ambling nag. Johnson.

hobbyhorsical.c: Hobbyhorsical Hob`by*hors"ic*al (?), n. Pertaining to, or having, a hobby or whim; eccentric; whimsical.[Colloq.] Sterne.

hobgoblin.c: Hobgoblin Hob"gob`lin (?), n. [See 2d Hob, and Goblin.] A frightful goblin; an imp; a bugaboo; also, a name formerly given to the household spirit, Robin Goodfellow. Macaulay.

hobiler.c: Hobiler Hob"i*ler (?), n.[See 2d Hobbler.] A light horseman. See 2d Hobbler. [Obs.] Brande & C.

hobit.c: Hobit Ho"bit (?), n. [See Howitzer.] (Mil.) A small mortar on a gun carriage, in use before the howitzer.

hobnail.c: Hobnail Hob"nail` (?), n. [1st hob + nail.] 1. A short, sharp-pointed, large-headed nail, -- used in shoeing houses and for studding the soles of heavy shoes.
Hobnail Hob"nail`, v. t. To tread down roughly, as with hobnailed shoes.

hobnailed.c: Hobnailed Hob"nailed` (?), a. See with hobnails, as a shoe.

hobnob.c: Hobnob Hob"nob` (?), adv. [AS. habban to have + habban to have not; ne not + habban to have. See Have, and cf. Habnab.] 1. Have or have not; -- a familiar invitation to reciprocal drinking. Shak.
Hobnob Hob"nob`, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Hornobbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hornobbing.] 1. To drink familiarly (with another). [ Written also hob-a-nob.]
Hobnob Hob"nob`, n. Familiar, social intercourse. W. Black.

hobo.c: Hobo Ho"bo (?), n.; pl. Hobos or Hoboes (#). [Of uncertain origin.] A professional tramp; one who spends his life traveling from place to place, esp. by stealing rides on trains, and begging for a living. [U. S.] -- Ho"bo*ism (#), n.

hoboy.c: Hoboy Ho"boy (?), n. A hautboy or oboe. [Obs.]

hobsons.c: Hobson's choice Hob"son's choice" (?). A choice without an alternative; the thing offered or nothing.

hocco.c: Hocco Hoc"co (?), n. (Zool.) The crested curassow; -- called also royal pheasant. See Curassow.

hock.c: Hock Hock (?), n. [So called from Hochheim, in Germany.] A Rhenish wine, of a light yellow color, either sparkling or still. The name is also given indiscriminately to all Rhenish wines.
Hock Hock, v. t. 1. To disable by cutting the tendons of the hock; to hamstring; to hough.

hough.c: Hough Hock Hock, Hough (?), n. [ AS. h?h the heel; prob. akin to Icel. hāsinn hock sinew, Dan. hasc, G. hechse, hächse, LG. hacke, D. hak; also to L. coxa hip (cf. Cuisses), Skr. kaksha armpit. √12. Cf. Heel.] 1. (a) The joint in the hind limb of quadrupeds between the leg and shank, or tibia and tarsus, and corresponding to the ankle in man. (b) A piece cut by butchers, esp. in pork, from either the front or hind leg, just above the foot.
Hough Hough (?), n. Same as Hock, a joint.
Hough Hough, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Houghed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Houghing.] Same as Hock, to hamstring.
Hough Hough, n. [Cf. D. hak. Cf. Hack.] An adz; a hoe. [Obs.] Bp. Stillingfleet.
Hough Hough, v. t. To cut with a hoe. [Obs.] Johnson.

hockamore.c: Hockamore Hock"a*more (?), n. [See 1st Hock.] A Rhenish wine. [Obs.] See Hock. Hudibras.

hockday.c: Hockday Hock"day` (?), n. [Cf. AS. hōcor mockery, scorn.] A holiday commemorating the expulsion of the Danes, formerly observed on the second Tuesday after Easter; -- called also hocktide. [Eng.] [Written also hokeday.]

hockey.c: Hockey Hock"ey (?), n. [From Hook, n.] 1. A game in which two parties of players, armed with sticks curved or hooked at the end, attempt to drive any small object (as a ball or a bit of wood) toward opposite goals.

hockle.c: Hockle Hoc"kle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hockled(?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hockling (?).] [From 2d Hock.] 1. To hamstring; to hock; to hough. Hanmer.

hocus.c: Hocus Ho"cus (?), v. t. [See Hocus-pocus.] 1. To deceive or cheat. Halliwell.
Hocus Ho"cus, n. 1. One who cheats or deceives. South.

hocuspocus.c: Hocus-pocus Ho"cus-po"cus (?), n. [Prob. invented by jugglers in imitation of Latin. Cf. Hoax, Hocus.] 1. A term used by magicians or conjurers in pretended incantations.
Hocus-pocus Ho"cus-po"cus, v. t. To cheat. [Colloq.] L'Estrange.

hod.c: Hod Hod (hŏd), n. [Prov. E. for hold, i. e., that which holds. See Hold.] 1. A kind of wooden tray with a handle, having V-shaped trough, made of wood or metal, attached to a long handle and usually carried over the shoulder; it is a tool used by construction workers for carrying bricks or mortar.

hoddengray.c: Hoddengray Hod"den*gray` (?), a. [Perh. akin to E. hoiden rustic, clownish.] Applied to coarse cloth made of undyed wool, formerly worn by Scotch peasants. [Scot.]

hoddy.c: Hoddy Hod"dy (?), n. [Prob. for hooded.] (Zool.) See Dun crow, under Dun, a.

hoddydoddy.c: Hoddydoddy Hod"dy*dod`dy (?), n. [Prob. E. also hoddypeke, hoddypoule, hoddymandoddy.] An awkward or foolish person. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

hodgepodge.c: Hodgepodge Hodge"podge` (?), n. A mixed mass; a medley. See Hotchpot. Johnson.

hodgkins.c: Hodgkin's disease Hodg`kin's dis*ease" (?). (Med.) A morbid condition characterized by progressive anæmia and enlargement of the lymphatic glands; -- first described by Dr. Hodgkin, an English physician.

hodiernal.c: Hodiernal Hodiern { Ho"di*ern (?), Ho`di*er"nal (?), } a. [L. hodiernus, fr. hodie today.] Of this day; belonging to the present day. [R.] Boyle. Quart. Rev.

hodman.c: Hodman Hod"man (?), n.; pl. Hodmen(?). A man who carries a hod; a mason's tender.

hodograph.c: Hodograph Hod"o*graph (?), n. [Gr.? path + graph.] (Math.) A curve described by the moving extremity of a line the other end of which is fixed, this line being constantly parallel to the direction of motion of, and having its length constantly proportional to the velocity of, a point moving in any path; -used in investigations respecting central forces.

hodometer.c: hodometer ho*dom"e*ter (ho*dŏm"e*tẽr), n. [Gr. "odo`metron, "odo`metros, an instrument for measuring distance; "odo`s way, path, road + me`tron measure: cf. F. odométre, hodométre. See also odometer.] A device for measuring the length of a path, consisting of a wheel of known circumference attached to a rod held in the hand, and pushed along a surface, which is usually the ground or a floor. The number of times the wheel makes a complete circle multiplied by the circumference is a measure of the length of the path traversed. It may be used to measure distances on curved as well as straight paths. A variant which registers the miles and rods traversed is sometimes used by surveyors.

hoe.c: Hoe Hoe (?), n. [OF. hoe, F. houe; of German origin, cf. OHG. houwa, howa, G. haue, fr. OHG. houwan to hew. See Hew to cut.] 1. A tool chiefly for digging up weeds, and arranging the earth about plants in fields and gardens. It is made of a flat blade of iron or steel having an eye or tang by which it is attached to a wooden handle at an acute angle.

Hoe Hoe, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hoed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hoeing.] [Cf. F. houer.] To cut, dig, scrape, turn, arrange, or clean, with a hoe; as, to hoe the earth in a garden; also, to clear from weeds, or to loosen or arrange the earth about, with a hoe; as, to hoe corn.
Hoe Hoe, v. i. To use a hoe; to labor with a hoe.

hoecake.c: Hoecake Hoe"cake` (?), n. A cake of Indian meal, water, and salt, baked before the fire or in the ashes; -- so called because often cooked on a hoe. [Southern U.S.]

hoemother.c: Hoemother Hoe"moth`er (?), n. [A local Orkney name; cf. Icel. hār.] (Zool.) The basking or liver shark; -- called also homer. See Liver shark, under Liver.

hoful.c: Hoful Ho"ful (?), a. [AS. hogful, hohful, fr. hogu care, anxiety.] Careful; wary. [Obs.] Stapleton.

hog.c: Hog Hog (hŏg), n. [Prob. akin to E. hack to cut, and meaning orig., a castrated boar; cf. also W. hwch swine, sow, Armor. houc'h, hoc'h. Cf. Haggis, Hogget, and Hoggerel.] 1. (Zool.) A quadruped of the genus Sus, and allied genera of Suidæ; esp., the domesticated varieties of Sus scrofa, kept for their fat and meat, called, respectively, lard and pork; swine; porker; specifically, a castrated boar; a barrow.
Hog Hog, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hogged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hogging.] 1. To cut short like bristles; as, to hog the mane of a horse. Smart.
Hog Hog, v. i. (Naut.) To become bent upward in the middle, like a hog's back; -- said of a ship broken or strained so as to have this form.

hogback.c: Hogback Hog"back` (?), n. 1. (Arch.) An upward curve or very obtuse angle in the upper surface of any member, as of a timber laid horizontally; -- the opposite of camber.

hogchain.c: Hogchain Hog"chain` (?), n. A chain or tie rod, in a boat or barge, to prevent the vessel from hogging.

hogchoker.c: Hogchoker Hog"chok`er (?), n. (Zool.) An American sole (Achirus lineatus syn. Achirus achirus), related to the European sole, but of no market value.

hogcote.c: Hogcote Hog"cote` (?), n. A shed for swine; a sty.

hogfish.c: Hogfish Hog"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A large West Indian and Florida food fish (Lachnolæmus). (b) The pigfish or sailor's choice. (c) An American fresh-water fish; the log perch. (d) A large, red, spiny-headed, European marine fish (Scorpæna scrofa).

hogframe.c: Hogframe Hog"frame` (?), n. (Steam Vessels) A trussed frame extending fore and aft, usually above deck, and intended to increase the longitudinal strength and stiffness. Used chiefly in American river and lake steamers. Called also hogging frame, and hogback.

hogged.c: Hogged Hogged (?), a. (Naut.) Broken or strained so as to have an upward curve between the ends. See Hog, v. i.

hogger.c: Hogger Hog"ger (?), n. A stocking without a foot, worn by coal miners at work.

hoggerel.c: Hoggerel Hog"ger*el (?), n. [From the same source as hog; prob. orig., a sheep clipped the first year. See Hog.] A sheep of the second year. [Written also hogrel.] Ash.

hoggerpipe.c: Hogger-pipe Hog"ger-pipe` (hŏg"gẽr-pīp`), n. (Mining) The upper terminal pipe of a mining pump. Raymond.

hoggerpump.c: Hogger-pump Hog"ger-pump" (hŏg"gẽr-pŭmp`), n. (Mining) The top pump in the pit. Raymond.

hoggery.c: Hoggery Hog"ger*y (?), n. Hoggish character or manners; selfishness; greed; beastliness.

hogget.c: Hogget Hog"get (?), n. [See Hog, and Hoggerel.] 1. A young boar of the second year.

hogging.c: Hogging Hog"ging (?), n. (Naut.) Drooping at the ends; arching;-in distinction from sagging.

hoggish.c: Hoggish Hog"gish (?), a. Swinish; gluttonous; filthy; selfish. -- Hog"gish*ly, adv. -- Hog"gish*ness, n.

hogh.c: Hogh Hogh (hō), n. [Icel. haugr hill, mound; akin to E. high. See High.] A hill; a cliff. [Obs.] Spenser.

hogherd.c: Hogherd Hog"herd (?), n. A swineherd. W. Browne.

hogmanay.c: Hogmanay Hog`ma*nay" (?), n. The old name, in Scotland, for the last day of the year, on which children go about singing, and receive a dole of bread or cakes; also, the entertainment given on that day to a visitor, or the gift given to an applicant. [Scot.]

hognosesnake.c: Hognosesnake Hog"nose`snake" (?). (Zool.) A harmless North American snake of the genus Heterodon, esp. Heterodon platyrhynos; -- called also puffing adder, blowing adder, and sand viper.

hognut.c: Hognut Hog"nut` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) The pignut. See Hickory. (b) In England, the Bunium flexuosum, a tuberous plant.

hogo.c: Hogo Ho"go (?), n. [Corrupted from F. haut goût.] High flavor; strong scent. [Obs.] Halliwell.

hogpen.c: Hogpen Hog"pen` (?), n. A pen or sty for hogs.

hogreeve.c: Hogreeve Hog"reeve` (?), n. [See Reeve.] A civil officer charged with the duty of impounding hogs running at large. [New Eng.] Bartlett.

hogringer.c: Hogringer Hog"ring`er (?), n. One who puts rings into the snouts of hogs.

hogscore.c: Hogscore Hog"score` (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Curling) A distance line drawn across the rink or course between the middle line and the tee. [Scot.]

hogshead.c: Hogshead Hogs"head (?), n. [D. okshoofd; akin to Sw. oxhufvud, Dan. oxehoved, G. oxhoft; apparently meaning orig., ox head, but it is not known why this name was given. Cf. Ox, Head.] 1. An English measure of capacity, containing 63 wine gallons, or about 52½ imperial gallons; a half pipe.

hogskin.c: Hogskin Hog"skin` (?), n. Leather tanned from a hog's skin. Also used adjectively.

hogsty.c: Hogsty Hog"sty` (?), n.; pl. Hogsties (?). A pen, house, or inclosure, for hogs.

hogweed.c: Hogweed Hog"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A common weed (Ambrosia artemisiæge). See Ambrosia, 3. (b) In England, the Heracleum Sphondylium.

hoiden.c: Hoiden Hoi"den (?), n. [OE. hoydon a lout, rustic, OD. heyden a heathen, gypsy, vagabond, D. heiden, fr. OD. heyde heath, D. heide. See Heathen, Heath.] [Written also hoyden.] 1. A rude, clownish youth. [Obs.] Milton.
Hoiden Hoi"den, a. Rustic; rude; bold. Younq.
Hoiden Hoi"den, v. i. To romp rudely or indecently. Swift.

hoidenhood.c: Hoidenhood Hoi"den*hood (?), n. State of being a hoiden.

hoidenish.c: Hoidenish Hoi"den*ish, a. Like, or appropriate to, a hoiden.

hoise.c: Hoise Hoise (?), v. t. [See Hoist.] To hoist. [Obs.]

hoist.c: Hoist Hoist (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hoisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Hoisting.] [OE. hoise, hyse, OD. hyssen, D. hijshen; akin to LG. hissen, Dan. hisse, Sw. hissa.] To raise; to lift; to elevate; esp., to raise or lift to a desired elevation, by means of tackle, as a sail, a flag, a heavy package or weight.
Hoist Hoist, n. 1. That by which anything is hoisted; the apparatus for lifting goods.

hoistaway.c: Hoistaway Hoist"a*way` (?), n. A mechanical lift. See Elevator.

hoistway.c: Hoistway Hoist"way` (?), n. An opening for the hoist, or elevator, in the floor of a wareroom.

hoit.c: Hoit Hoit (?), v. i. [Gf. W. hoetian to dally, dandle.] To leap; to caper; to romp noisily. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

hoitytoity.c: Hoity-toity Hoi"ty-toi`ty (?), a. [From Hoit.] Thoughtless; giddy; flighty; also, haughty; patronizing; as, to be in hoity-toity spirits, or to assume hoity-toity airs; used also as an exclamation, denoting surprise or disapprobation, with some degree of contempt.

hoker.c: Hoker Ho"ker (?), n. [AS. hōcor.] Scorn; derision; abusive talk. [Obs.] -- Ho"ker*ly, adv. [Obs.] Chaucer.

holarctic.c: Holarctic Hol"arc*tic (?), a. [Holo- + arctic.] Of or pert. to the arctic regions collectively; specif. (Zoögeography), designating a realm or region including the northern parts of the Old and the New World. It comprises the Palearctic and Nearctic regions or subregions.

holaspidean.c: Holaspidean Hol`as*pid"e*an (?), a. [Holo- + Gr.?,?, shield.] (Zool.) Having a single series of large scutes on the posterior side of the tarsus; -- said of certain birds.

holcad.c: Holcad Hol"cad (?), n. [Gr. 'olka`s, -a`dos, a ship which is towed, a ship of burden, fr. 'e`lkein to draw. Gf. Hulk.] A large ship of burden, in ancient Greece. Mitford.

hold.c: Hold Hold (hōld), n. [D. hol hole, hollow. See Hole.] (Naut.) The whole interior portion of a vessel below the lower deck, in which the cargo is stowed.

Hold Hold, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Held (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Holding. Holden (?), p. p., is obs. in elegant writing, though still used in legal language.] [OE. haldan, D. houden, OHG. hoten, Icel. halda, Dan. holde, Sw. hålla, Goth. haldan to feed, tend (the cattle); of unknown origin. Gf. Avast, Halt, Hod.]
Hold Hold, v. i. In general, to keep one's self in a given position or condition; to remain fixed. Hence:

Hold Hold (hōld), n. 1. The act of holding, as in or with the hands or arms; the manner of holding, whether firm or loose; seizure; grasp; clasp; grip; possession; -- often used with the verbs take and lay.

holdback.c: Holdback Hold"back` (?), n. 1. Check; hindrance; restraint; obstacle.

holder.c: Holder Hold"er, (?) n. One who is employed in the hold of a vessel.
Holder Hold"er, n. 1. One who, or that which, holds.

holderforth.c: Holder-forth Hold"er-forth` (?), n. One who speaks in public; an haranguer; a preacher. See hold forth (b) under hold. Addison.

holdfast.c: Holdfast Hold"fast` (?), n. 1. Something used to secure and hold in place something else, as a long flat-headed nail, a catch a hook, a clinch, a clamp, etc.; hence, a support. “His holdfast was gone.” Bp. Montagu.

holding.c: Holding Hold"ing, n. 1. The act or state of sustaining, grasping, or retaining.

hole.c: Hole Hole (hōl), n. [OE. hol, hole, AS. hol, hole, cavern, from hol, a., hollow; akin to D. hol, OHG. hol, G. hohl, Dan. huul hollow, hul hole, Sw. hål, Icel. hola; prob. from the root of AS. helan to conceal. See Hele, Hell, and cf. Hold of a ship.] 1. A hollow place or cavity; an excavation; a pit; an opening in or through a solid body, a fabric, etc.; a perforation; a rent; a fissure.
Hole Hole (?), v. t. [AS. holian. See Hole, n.] 1. To cut, dig, or bore a hole or holes in; as, to hole a post for the insertion of rails or bars. Chapman.
Hole Hole, v. i. To go or get into a hole. B. Jonson.
Hole in the air Hole in the air. (Aëronautics) same as Air hole, above; an air pocket.

holethnic.c: Holethnic Hol*eth"nic (?), a. Of or pertaining to a holethnos or parent race.

holethnos.c: Holethnos Hol*eth"nos (?), n. [Holo + Gr.? race.] A parent stock or race of people, not yet divided into separate branches or tribes.

holiday.c: Holiday Hol"i*day (?), n. [Holy + day.] 1. A consecrated day; religious anniversary; a day set apart in honor of some person, or in commemoration of some event. See Holyday.
Holiday Hol`i*day, a. 1. Of or pertaining to a festival; cheerful; joyous; gay. Shak.

holily.c: Holily Ho"li*ly (?), adv. [From Holy.] 1. Piously; with sanctity; in a holy manner.

holiness.c: Holiness Ho"li*ness, n. [AS. hālignes.] 1. The state or quality of being holy; perfect moral integrity or purity; freedom from sin; sanctity; innocence.

holing.c: Holing Hol"ing (?), n. [See Hole a hollow.] (Mining) Undercutting in a bed of coal, in order to bring down the upper mass. Raymond.

holla.c: Holla Hol"la (?), interj. [F. hola; ho ho + là there, fr. L. illac that way, there. Cf. Hollo.] Hollo.
Holla Hol"la, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Hollaed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hollaing.] See Hollo, v. i.

holland.c: Holland Hol"land (?), n. A kind of linen first manufactured in Holland; a linen fabric used for window shades, children's garments, etc.; as, brown or unbleached hollands.

hollandaise.c: Hollandaise Hollandaise sauce { Hol`lan*daise" sauce, or Hol`lan*daise" } (?), n. [F. hollandaise, fem. of hollandais Dutch.] (Cookery) A sauce consisting essentially of a seasoned emulsion of butter and yolk of eggs with a little lemon juice or vinegar.

hollander.c: Hollander Hol"land*er (?), prop. n. 1. A native or one of the people of Holland; a Dutchman.

hollandish.c: Hollandish Hol"land*ish, a. Relating to Holland; Dutch.

hollands.c: Hollands Hol"lands (?), n. 1. Gin made in Holland.

hollo.c: Hollo Hol*lo" (?), interj. & n. [See Halloo, and cf. Holla.] Ho there; stop; attend; hence, a loud cry or a call to attract attention; a halloo.
Hollo Hol"lo (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Holloed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Holloing.] [See Hollo, interj., and cf. Halloo.] To call out or exclaim; to halloo.

holloa.c: Holloa Hol*loa" (?), interj., n. & v. i. Same as Hollo.

hollow.c: Hollow Hol"low (?), a. [OE. holow, holgh, holf, AS. holh a hollow, hole. Cf. Hole.] 1. Having an empty space or cavity, natural or artificial, within a solid substance; not solid; excavated in the interior; as, a hollow tree; a hollow sphere.
Hollow Hol"low (?), n. 1. A cavity, natural or artificial; an unfilled space within anything; a hole, a cavern; an excavation; as the hollow of the hand or of a tree.
Hollow Hol"low, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Hollowed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Hollowing.] To make hollow, as by digging, cutting, or engraving; to excavate. “Trees rudely hollowed.” Dryden.
Hollow Hol"low, adv. Wholly; completely; utterly; -- chiefly after the verb to beat, and often with all; as, this story beats the other all hollow. See All, adv. [Colloq.]
Hollow Hol"low (?), v. i. To shout; to hollo.
Hollow Hol"low, v. t. To urge or call by shouting.

hollowhearted.c: Hollow-hearted Hol"low-heart`ed (?), a. Insincere; deceitful; not sound and true; having a cavity or decayed spot within.

hollowhorned.c: Hollow-horned Hol"low-horned` (?), a. (Zool.) Having permanent horns with a bony core, as cattle.

hollowness.c: Hollowness Hol"low*ness, n. 1. State of being hollow. Bacon.

holluschickie.c: Holluschickie Hol"lus*chick`ie (?), n. sing. & pl. [Prob. of Russ. goluishka bare of possessions, offspring, etc., fr. goluiĭ naked.] (Zool.) A young male fur seal, esp. one from three to six years old; -- called also bachelor, because prevented from breeding by the older full-grown males.

holly.c: Holly Hol"ly (hŏl"ly̆), n. [OE holi, holin, AS. holen, holegn; akin to D. & G. hulst, OHG. huls hulis, W. celyn, Armor. kelen, Gael. cuilionn, Ir. cuileann. Cf. 1st Holm, Hulver.] 1. (Bot.) A tree or shrub of the genus Ilex. The European species (Ilex Aquifolium) is best known, having glossy green leaves, with a spiny, waved edge, and bearing berries that turn red or yellow about Michaelmas.

hollyhock.c: Hollyhock Hol"ly*hock (?), n. [OE. holihoc; holi holy + hoc mallow, AS. hoc; cf. W. hocys mallows, hocys bendigaid hollyhock, lit., blessed mallow. Prob. so named because brought from the Holy Land. See Holy.] (Bot.) A species of Althæa (Althæa rosea), bearing flowers of various colors; -- called also rose mallow.

holm.c: Holm Holm (hōm; 277), n. [OE., prob. from AS. holen holly; as the holly is also called holm. See Holly.] (Bot.) A common evergreen oak, of Europe (Quercus Ilex); -- called also ilex, and holly.
Holm Holm (hōm), n. [AS. holm, usually meaning, sea, water; akin to Icel. hōlmr, holmr, an island, Dan. holm, Sw. holme, G. holm, and prob. to E. hill. Cf. Hill.]

holmium.c: Holmium ‖Hol"mi*um (?), n. [NL., from Stockholm.] (Chem.) A rare element of atomic number 67 said to be contained in gadolinite. Chemical symbol Ho. Atomic weight 164.93. Valence +3. It was detected by spectral absorption bands in 1878 by the Delafontaine and Soret, who called it "Element X". Later the Swedish chemist Cleve independently discovered it in erbia, and named it after his native city Stockholm. The first preparation of pure Holmia, the yellow oxide, was not made until 1911. HCP61 -- Hol"mic (#), a.

holmos.c: Holmos ‖Hol"mos (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?.] (Greek & Etrus. Antiq.) A name given to a vase having a rounded body; esp.: (a) A closed vessel of nearly spherical form on a high stem or pedestal. Fairholt. (b) A drinking cup having a foot and stem.

holo.c: Holo- Hol"o- (?). A combining form fr. Gr. "o`los whole.

holoblast.c: Holoblast Hol"o*blast (?), n. [Holo + -blast.] (Biol.) an ovum composed entirely of germinal matter. See Meroblast.

holoblastic.c: Holoblastic Hol`o*blas"tic (?), a. (Biol.) Undergoing complete segmentation; composed entirely of germinal matter, the whole of the yolk undergoing fission; -- opposed to meroblastic.

holocaust.c: Holocaust Hol"o*caust (?), n. [L. holocaustum, Gr.?, neut. of?,?, burnt whole; "o`los whole + kaysto`s burnt, fr. kai`ein to burn (cf. Caustic): cf. F. holocauste.] 1. A burnt sacrifice; an offering, the whole of which was consumed by fire, among the Jews and some pagan nations. Milton.

holocephali.c: Holocephali ‖Hol`o*ceph"a*li (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr. "o`los whole + kefalh` head.] (Zool.) An order of elasmobranch fishes, including, among living species, only the chimæras; -- called also Holocephala. See Chimæra; also Illustration in Appendix.

holocryptic.c: Holocryptic Hol`o*cryp"tic (?), a. [Holo- + Gr. kry`ptein to conceal.] Wholly or completely concealing; incapable of being deciphered.

holocrystalline.c: Holocrystalline Hol`o*crys"tal*line (?), a. [Holo + crystalline.] (Min.) Completely crystalline; -- said of a rock like granite, all the constituents of which are crystalline.

holograph.c: Holograph Hol"o*graph (?), n. [L. holographus entirely autograph, Gr. "olo`grafos; "o`los whole + gra`fein to write: cf. F. holographe, olographe.] 1. A document, as a letter, deed, or will, wholly in the handwriting of the person from whom it proceeds and whose act it purports to be.

holographic.c: Holographic Hol`o*graph"ic (?), a. 1. Of the nature of a holograph; pertaining to holographs.

holohedral.c: Holohedral Hol`o*he"dral (?), a. [Holo- + Gr.? seat, base, fr.? to sit.] (Crystallog.) Having all the planes required by complete symmetry, -- in opposition to hemihedral.

holohemihedral.c: Holohemihedral Hol`o*hem`i*he"dral (?), a. [Holo- + hemihedral.] (Crystallog.) Presenting hemihedral forms, in which all the sectants have halt the whole number of planes. Dana.

holometabola.c: Holometabola ‖Hol`o*me*tab"o*la (?), n. pl. [NL. See Holo-, and Metabola.] (Zool.) Those insects which have a complete metamorphosis; metabola.

holometabolic.c: Holometabolic Hol`o*met`a*bol"ic (?), a. (Zool.) Having a complete metamorphosis; -- said of certain insects, as the butterflies and bees.

holometer.c: Holometer Ho*lom"e*ter (?), n. [Holo + -meter: cf. F. holometre.] An instrument for making all kinds of angular measurements.

holophanerous.c: Holophanerous Hol`o*phan"er*ous (?), a. [Holo + Gr.? visible, fr.? to appear.] (Zool.) Same as Holometabolic.

holophotal.c: Holophotal Hol`o*pho"tal (?), a. [Holo + Gr.?,?, light.] (Opt.) Causing no loss of light; -- applied to reflectors which throw back the rays of light without perceptible loss.

holophote.c: Holophote Hol"o*phote (?), n. A lamp with lenses or reflectors to collect the rays of light and throw them in a given direction; -- used in lighthouses.

holophrastic.c: Holophrastic Hol`o*phras"tic (?), a. [Holo + Gr.? to speak: cf. F. holophrastique.] Expressing a phrase or sentence in a single word, -- as is the case in the aboriginal languages of America.

holophytic.c: Holophytic Hol`o*phyt"ic (?), a. [Holo + Gr.? a plant.] Wholly or distinctively vegetable.

holorhinal.c: Holorhinal Hol`o*rhi"nal (?), a. [Holo + Gr.?, nose.] (Anat.) Having the nasal bones contiguous.

holosiderite.c: Holosiderite Hol`o*sid"er*ite (?), n. [Holo + siderite.] (Min.) Meteoric iron; a meteorite consisting of metallic iron without stony matter.

holostean.c: Holostean Ho*los"te*an (?), a. (Zool.) Pertaining to the Holostei.

holostei.c: Holostei ‖Ho*los"te*i (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. "o`los whole +? a bone.] (Zool.) An extensive division of ganoids, including the gar pike, bowfin, etc.; the bony ganoids. See Illustration in Appendix.

holosteric.c: Holosteric Hol`o*ster"ic (?), a. [Holo + Gr.stereo`s solid.] Wholly solid; -- said of a barometer constructed of solid materials to show the variations of atmospheric pressure without the use of liquids, as the aneroid.

holostomata.c: Holostomata ‖Hol`o*stom"a*ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. "o`los whole + sto`ma, -atos, mouth.] (Zool.) An artificial division of gastropods, including those that have an entire aperture.

holostomatous.c: Holostomatous Hol`o*stom"a*tous (?), a. (Zool.) Having an entire aperture; -- said of many univalve shells.

holostome.c: Holostome Hol"o*stome (?), n. [Holo + Gr. sto`ma mouth.] (Zool.) One of the Holostomata.

holostraca.c: Holostraca ‖Ho*los"tra*ca (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. "o`los whole +? shell of a testacean.] (Zool.) A division of phyllopod Crustacea, including those that are entirely covered by a bivalve shell.

holothure.c: Holothure Hol"o*thure (?), n. [L. holothuria, pl., a sort of water polyp, Gr.?.] (Zool.) A holothurian.

holothurian.c: Holothurian Hol`o*thu"ri*an (?), a. (Zool.) Belonging to the Holothurioidea. -- n. One of the Holothurioidea.

holothurioidea.c: Holothurioidea ‖Hol`o*thu`ri*oi"de*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Holothure, and -oid.] (Zool.) One of the classes of echinoderms.

holotricha.c: Holotricha ‖Ho*lot"ri*cha (ho*lŏt"rĭ*kȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. "o`los whole + qri`x, tricho`s, a hair.] (Zool.) A group of ciliated Infusoria, having cilia all over the body.

holour.c: Holour Hol"our (?), n. [OF. holier.] A whoremonger. [Obs.] Chaucer.

holpen.c: Holpen Holp { Holp (?), Hol"pen (?), } imp. & p. p. of Help. [Obs.] Shak.

holstein.c: Holstein Hol"stein (?), n. (Zool.) One of a breed of cattle, originally from Schleswig-Holstein, valued for the large amount of milk produced by the cows. The color is usually black and white in irregular patches.

holster.c: Holster Hol"ster (?), n. [D. holster; skin to AS. heolstor den, cave, fr. helan to conceal, and to Icel. hulstr case, Goth. hulistr covering, veil, huljan to cover. √17. See Hele to cover, Hell, and cf. Housing, Houss.] A leather case for a pistol, carried by a horseman at the bow of his saddle, or worn on the person suspended from a belt or shoulder strap.

holt.c: Holt Holt (?), 3d pers. sing. pres. of Hold, contr. from holdeth. [Obs.] Chaucer.
